label: Who is William Derbyshire?
quote: Mrs. Straker tells us that Derbyshire was a friend of her husband’s

possibilities.value: a friend of Straker's, as Mrs. Straker says
possibilities.quote: Derbyshire was a friend of her husband’s

reasoning.text: Derbyshire's letters come to Straker's own house, and a bill made out to Derbyshire was in Straker's own pocket. The 'friend' may be Straker under another name.

label: Who wore the costly costumes on the milliner's account?
quote: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes

possibilities.quote: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes

possibilities.value: a woman Straker kept without his wife's knowledge

reasoning.text: The bill was in Straker's pocket, yet his wife says she never had such a dress. Costly clothes he paid for under another name went to some other woman.

label: Why did Straker carry a candle and matches on his walk to the stables?

possibilities.value: by habit, or to light his pipe
to have a small light somewhere out on the moor

reasoning.text: The stable had its own light and a lad on watch. A man who takes a candle out on a rainy night expects to need a light somewhere else, out of the wind.

value: to make some fine cut on the horse

reasoning.text: It is a cataract knife, made for delicate work. Its cork guard was found off, lying beside the body. A man snatching up a weapon would not cap it, and in a sudden fight he would not stop to uncap it. The horse was there in the hollow.

value: to do something to the horse himself

reasoning.text: He took a delicate surgeon's blade and a candle, and he died in the hollow where the horse had been, with his coat off and the knife uncapped.

asserts.value: to use the knife as a weapon to defend himself

set.pick: a friend of Straker's, as Mrs. Straker says
